title: Social Sciences · Seq 3 Social sciences and their methods

questions.stem: About the history of the social sciences:
options: Their emergence was helped by the Industrial and French revolutions
They emerged as a distinct form of research in the 18th century
They appeared as a distinct discipline in the 20th century
Their origins can be traced back to the ancient Greeks
questions.explanation: 18th century (Age of Enlightenment, age of revolutions): social philosophy gave way to a scientific emphasis.

questions.stem: Positivism was first articulated by:
options: Thomas Kuhn
Auguste Comte
Émile Durkheim
Max Weber
questions.explanation: Comte, best described in his 1848 work A General View of Positivism.

questions.stem: About positivism as a mode of knowledge:
options: It rejects the scientific method
It moved away from metaphysical speculation
It focuses on facts and falsifiable statements about the empirical world
It is knowledge based on actual positive sense experience
questions.explanation: Positivism focuses on the scientific method's ability to produce facts and falsifiable statements.

questions.stem: According to Burrell and Morgan (1979):
options: Epistemology refers to our assumptions about the best way to study the world
Epistemology is the study of human emotions
Ontology refers to our assumptions about how we see the world
Ontology refers to the best method to collect data
questions.explanation: Ontology: social order or constant change? Epistemology: objective or subjective approach?

questions.stem: Statistical analysis was first incorporated into social scientific writings with:
options: Kuhn's The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962)
Comte's A General View of Positivism (1848)
Burrell and Morgan's Sociological Paradigms (1979)
Émile Durkheim's Suicide (1897)
questions.explanation: Before that, early social science relied heavily on human observation.

questions.stem: Compared with the natural sciences, the social sciences tend to be:
options: Less accurate
Less deterministic
Independent of the person making the observations
Less unambiguous
questions.explanation: Independence from the observer is a feature of the natural sciences.

questions.stem: About inductive and deductive research:
options: Inductive research is also called theory-building research
Inductive research infers theoretical concepts and patterns from observed data
Deductive research tests concepts and patterns from theory using new empirical data
Deductive research is also called theory-building research
questions.explanation: Deductive = theory-testing (and possibly refining, improving, extending the theory).

questions.stem: Inductive (theory-building) research is most valuable when:
options: There are few prior theories or explanations
The theory has been proven
Data are already fully analysed
There are many competing theories of the same phenomenon
questions.explanation: Deductive research is more productive when many competing theories exist.

questions.stem: The word "paradigm" was popularized by:
options: McDonald (1993)
Auguste Comte (1848)
Saunders et al. (2009)
Thomas Kuhn (1962)
questions.explanation: In The Structure of Scientific Revolutions.

questions.stem: Match the paradigm to its emphasis:
options: Postmodernism — value-free, objective truth
Positivism — objectivity, knowability and deductive logic
Social constructionism — truth as varying, socially constructed and ever-changing
Critical paradigm — power, inequality and social change
questions.explanation: Postmodernism claims there is no objective, knowable truth; a value-free sociology is the positivist aim.

questions.stem: The interpretivist paradigm:
options: Stresses understanding differences among humans as social actors
Calls for a value-free sociology
Emphasizes research among people rather than objects
Uses the analogy of the theatre, where actors interpret their parts
questions.explanation: Saunders, Lewis & Thornhill (2009). Value-free sociology is positivism.

questions.stem: The course illustrates the social constructionist idea that meaning is constructed socially with:
options: Durkheim's study of suicide
Hand gestures that vary across regions of the world
Two students from different academic fields
Birth and marriage certificates
questions.explanation: Different meanings of hand gestures show meaning is constructed socially and collectively. The two students illustrate interpretivism.

questions.stem: Which paradigm states that social science can never be truly objective or value-free and should seek social change?
options: Social constructionism
Positivism
Interpretivism
Critical paradigm
questions.explanation: The critical paradigm, unlike positivism.

questions.stem: Mental attitudes required for successful scientific research:
options: Prejudice
Objectivity
Scepticism
Curiosity
questions.explanation: Curiosity, scepticism and objectivity.

questions.stem: In the course's approach to a social-science problem:
options: Drawing conclusions comes before collecting data
Choosing a research design is described as the crux of the research process
After analysing the results the hypothesis can be confirmed, rejected or modified
Reviewing the literature comes after defining the problem
questions.explanation: Order: observe → define problem → review literature → observe more → framework & hypothesis → design → collect data → analyse → conclude.

questions.stem: Match the method to its example:
options: Historical method — collecting birth and marriage certificates
Comparative and cross-cultural method — comparing how different societies meet similar needs
Case method — detailed study of a single person, a town or a whole country
Case method — tracing past developments of a social situation
questions.explanation: Tracing past developments is the historical method.

questions.stem: Qualitative research methods listed in the course:
options: Correlational research
Case study research
One-on-one online interview and content analysis
Ethnographic research and focus groups
questions.explanation: Correlational research is one of the 4 quantitative methods (survey, correlational, causal-comparative, experimental).

questions.stem: About primary and secondary research:
options: Primary research is conducted by the researchers themselves
Primary data are collected first-hand and are highly accurate
Newspapers, reports and audiovisual evidence are secondary data
Secondary research always uses close-ended questionnaires sent by the researcher
questions.explanation: Secondary research uses information already collected by others.

questions.stem: Why is it difficult to discover exact laws governing social life?
options: Social scientists routinely use controlled experiments
There is a human element in any social situation
Laws are not measurable (e.g. satisfaction, democracy)
Society is extremely complex
questions.explanation: Investigators seldom employ controlled experiments; they use careful observation and abstraction.

questions.stem: Recasting a research problem so that it fits one's favourite method (e.g. survey research) is called:
options: Pursuing research fads
Favored research methods
Blind data mining
Unresearchable problems
questions.explanation: Methods should be chosen to fit the problem, not the other way around.

questions.stem: "Blind data mining" means:
options: Collecting data first with available instruments, then figuring out what to do with it
Studying problems that cannot be answered with evidence
Choosing popular topics with a limited shelf life
Choosing pet problems that interest only the researcher
questions.explanation: B = research fads, C = insufficiently motivated questions, D = unresearchable problems.
